title: Outlining
lede: An outline is where the thinking happens. Five minutes of structure saves an hour of rewriting, and the right shape makes your argument hit harder.

sections.md:
## Why outline
Writing a good essay means solving two problems at once: **what to say** and **how to say it**. An outline splits them. You decide the **order of ideas** first, when it's cheap to move things around, and then you only worry about sentences.

The best outlines are short: a thesis and one line per paragraph. If you can't write the one-line version, you're not ready to write the paragraph.

## The basic skeleton
**I. Introduction**: hook, context, **thesis**
**II. Body paragraph 1**: topic sentence (reason 1) → evidence → explanation
**III. Body paragraph 2**: topic sentence (reason 2) → evidence → explanation
**IV. Body paragraph 3**: topic sentence (reason 3) → evidence → explanation
**V. Conclusion**: thesis in new words → why it matters

This is the **five-paragraph essay**. It's a training scaffold, like a heavy bag: great for drilling structure, but real essays bend it. Use as many body paragraphs as your argument needs, one idea each.

## Order matters: pick a structure
| Structure | Use it when | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| **Strongest last** (climactic) | arguing; you want to end with your best punch | good → better → best |
| **Chronological** | telling what happened, or a process | first → next → finally |
| **Problem → solution** | proposing a change | what's wrong → why → fix → why the fix works |
| **Compare (point by point)** | comparing two things in detail | cost: A vs B → speed: A vs B → risk: A vs B |
| **Compare (block)** | comparing two things simply | all of A → all of B |
| **Claim → counterclaim → rebuttal** | persuading skeptics | my point → their best objection → why I'm still right |

For arguments, **strongest last** is standard; some writers put the second-best point first and the best last, so the essay opens and closes strong.

sections.q: You're comparing two trucks on price, fuel economy and reliability, in detail. Which structure keeps the comparison sharpest?
options: Block: all of truck A, then all of truck B
Point by point: price (A vs B), fuel (A vs B), reliability (A vs B)
sections.why: Point by point puts each matchup side by side, so readers never have to flip back to remember truck A.

sections.md:
## One idea per paragraph
Each body paragraph proves **one** reason, stated in its **topic sentence**. Under it, every sentence should either give evidence for that reason or explain how the evidence proves it.

Test your outline: read only the topic sentences in order. They should form a mini-version of the whole essay. If one doesn't connect to the thesis, cut it or rewrite the thesis.

sections.title: Outline from a thesis
sections.problem: **Thesis:** *Every new trader should journal rule-breaks, because it exposes patterns, separates bad luck from bad behavior, and builds the discipline that strategy can't.*
steps: **Body 1, exposes patterns**: a journal shows that most losses cluster after big wins or at certain times. Evidence: example log.
**Body 2, luck vs behavior**: a losing trade that followed every rule is fine; a winning trade that broke rules is a warning. Evidence: two contrasting trades.
**Body 3, discipline (strongest)**: counting rule-breaks gives a number to improve, independent of P&L. Evidence: rule-break count falling over 8 weeks.
**Conclusion**: P&L is noisy; rule-breaks are in your control. Track what you control.
sections.answer: Four lines of planning. The essay now writes itself paragraph by paragraph.

sections.md:
## The reverse outline
After you draft, outline **backward**: write one line summarizing each paragraph *as written*. Then check:
- Does each paragraph have **one** main point?
- Do the points follow the thesis, in a logical order?
- Is anything repeated, missing or off-topic?

This is the fastest way to find structural problems in your own writing, which is otherwise very hard because you know what you *meant*.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Outlining sentences instead of ideas.** Keep it to short phrases.
- **Two ideas in one paragraph.** If the topic sentence needs an *and*, consider splitting it.
- **Saving the thesis for the end.** In argument and school writing, readers want the destination up front.
- **Treating the outline as a contract.** If drafting reveals a better order, change the outline.

practice.q: The main job of an outline is to…
options: decide the order of ideas before writing sentences

practice.q: In a classic body paragraph, what comes first?
practice.why: The topic sentence states the paragraph's one idea.

practice.q: For an argument, a common order for reasons is…
A how-to essay on setting up a trading chart should use…
practice.why: A process goes step by step.

options: after drafting, from what the paragraphs actually say
practice.why: It shows you what you actually wrote.

practice.q: Your topic sentence reads: "Cardio matters, and also nutrition is key." What's wrong?
practice.why: One paragraph, one idea. Split it.

practice.q: Proposing that your city add truck parking: which structure fits best?
practice.why: Show the problem, then argue for the fix.

practice.q: Reading only your topic sentences in order should give you…
options: a short version of the whole argument
practice.why: If they don't, the structure needs work.

practice.q: You're writing to persuade skeptical readers that same-day weigh-ins are better. Which structure handles skeptics best?
practice.why: Raising their strongest objection and answering it shows you've thought it through. Skeptics trust writers who face the other side.
practice.hint: Skeptics already have objections. What do you do with them?

practice.q: Your thesis has three reasons, but your reverse outline shows five body paragraphs, two of which are about a fourth idea. Best fix?
options: Either cut the two paragraphs or revise the thesis to include the fourth idea
practice.why: The thesis and body must match. Either the extra idea is off-topic (cut it) or it's important (add it to the thesis).
practice.hint: What's the rule about paragraphs that don't support the thesis?

practice.q: Reasons ranked by strength: B (strongest), C (weakest), A (middle). Using "open and close strong," which order?
practice.why: Second-best first (A), weakest buried in the middle (C), best last (B).
practice.hint: Put the weakest where it matters least.

practice.q: Point-by-point comparison of two fight camps on coaching, sparring partners and cost has how many body sections?
practice.why: One section per point of comparison, each covering **both** camps: coaching, sparring, cost = **3**.
practice.hint: Point by point organizes by the features, not by the camps.
